newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Infotech deal prospects murky on day one of WTO meet.
newsitem.headline: Infotech deal prospects murky on day one of WTO meet.

text.p: Prospects for a global deal to eliminate tariffs on a host of information technologies were murky on Monday as officials said much work lay ahead in the drive to conclude an agreement.
The United States has been pushing hard for a deal to be wrapped up by the end of the World Trade Organisation's (WTO) ministerial meeting on Friday with the strong backing of Japan.
Japan on Monday joined the U.S. in suggesting that Brussels was an obstacle to an information technology agreement (ITA).

Acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky, who would like to make a global ITA the crowning achievement of the first WTO ministerial meeting, said it would help businesses become more competitive in the global economy by putting lower-cost technologies and information into their hands.

"That's why we must reach an agreement this week," she said in a speech to the opening session of the WTO meeting. "Remaining issues are ripe for discussion. We have an historic opportunity to eliminate tariffs on these products. We must seize it."
Japan, a key player in the world infotech market, is also keen to see a deal forged.

"Everyone should recognise the importance of this tariff action because at the end of the day, it will be for everyone's benefit," a Japanese spokesman told reporters. "That's why we are very positive and hopeful that a general agreement will be made."
European Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan said an ITA pact was vital to the success of the WTO gathering, along with progress towards a WTO pact liberalising telecommunications markets.

"I should not have to say that we all have to make a further effort. But we do. If we do not make substantial progress on both issues this week, with new offers tabled, then our meeting will not be the big success we all want," Brittan told the WTO meeting.
Whether that success would elude the world trade body's grasp, however, remained unclear.
Singapore's Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong told reporters: "I think there will be an agreement but not an agreement on zero tariffs by 2000."
Developing countries want more flexibility on the timetable for eliminating tariffs on infotech products.
Australian deputy premier and trade minister Tim Fischer said there were still a lot of negotiations proceeding at the margins.
"I think there are a few balls up in the air at 12-noon on day one and we will have to wait and see," said Fischer.

The Japanese spokesman said he was "not that pessimistic" about prospects for a general agreement but pointed to Brussels as an obstacle. "The main obstacle is the European Union," he said, adding that Tokyo was concerned over an EU effort to link the elmination of tariffs to non-tariff issues, such as further liberalisation of government procurement.
"We believe it is important to abolish tariffs in semiconductors. Why bring in other issues -- that could be seen as just delaying tactics," the spokesman said of the EU stance.

One U.S. businessman lobbying for the ITA said he would be "very disappointed" if no deal was forged. "I am bullish but not cocky," said Aaron Cross, public policy director at International Business Machines (IBM).
Besides the question of non-tariff linkage, the ITA talks have been focusing on four types of products covering only two percent of the industry's global exports, officials said.

These four categories -- fibre optics, graphics display tubes, photocopiers and capacitors, which are circuits used in electronic goods -- represented only $13 billion of the $595 billion worth of IT products exported last year.
But officials say consensus on these issues is vital for a deal to be struck at the WTO gathering. The EU wants the products included in any IT agreement but the U.S. wants them left out.
